title: Xiaomi's Three Chips: Trading Resources for Time, Betting on an On-Device AI Paradigm Shift
dek: Xiaomi released three Xuanjie chips at once, aggressively betting on memory interconnect, 3D stacking, and an all-AI architecture. It's trading resources for time, betting on an on-device AI paradigm shift and vertical integration—but it still lags top-tier chip companies.
why: This episode offers an in-depth analysis of the technical choices and strategic logic behind Xiaomi's three chips. It's information-dense, with clear analogies for key technologies like memory interconnect and 3D stacking. Worth a listen for chip industry professionals and investors tracking Xiaomi.
who: Investors focused on Xiaomi's chip efforts, chip industry engineers, product managers, and tech professionals wanting to understand on-device AI trends.
skip: The first 3 minutes discussing the definition of self-developed chips can be skipped; jump straight to the technical analysis.

points.h: Chip capability is about system definition, not IP self-reliance
points.body: To judge whether a company can make chips, don't just count how many IP blocks it hand-crafts; look at how much system definition power it holds. Xiaomi's Xuanjie O1 uses ARM IP for CPU and GPU, but system integration and physical implementation are done in-house. Apple and Qualcomm excel at yearly iteration and continuous tape-outs—something latecomers lack. Xiaomi doesn't have a decade to learn slowly, so it chooses an aggressive path, advancing multiple high-risk technology lines simultaneously.

points.h: O1's poor energy efficiency stems from a missing shared water tank
points.body: The Xuanjie O1 lacks a system-level cache (SLC), causing power consumption to spike under heavy GPU load and hurting energy efficiency. An SLC is like a shared water tank in a residential complex: the closer data is to the compute units, the faster the access and the lower the power. The O1 has many GPU cores but limited DDR bandwidth, so many cores idle waiting for data—this is the bandwidth wall. The O3 adds a 16MB SLC, split into multiple cache blocks distributed across the chip, and designs an on-chip network scheduler to handle data consistency and access conflicts.

points.h: ARM's generic bus forced Xuanjie to build its own
points.body: ARM's off-the-shelf CHI+CMN solution is too generic, retaining compatibility and redundancy that hinder customization for Xuanjie. The O3 instead develops its own X-Ring unified fabric, compatible with CHI but defining its own interconnect protocol, along with a custom high-speed routing hub and memory controller. This reduces protocol conversion overhead and lets data decide cache placement and paths based on demand. Xiaomi claims protocol conversion overhead drops 75%, and static access latency is 82 nanoseconds—32% lower than the O1, even beating Apple's A19 Pro.

points.h: Compute bottleneck shifts from matrix multiplication to vector operations
points.body: The O3 adds AI units to every subsystem—CPU, GPU, ISP, etc.—so computation happens where the data resides, reducing data movement. The NPU core count drops from 6 to 4, but Tensor compute rises to 200 TOPS, because Xiaomi judges that the bottleneck for large models is shifting from matrix multiplication to vector operations like Softmax, quantization, and KV cache. The vector unit area is comparable to the Tensor unit, with 6.8 times the multiply-accumulate units of the O1, and it introduces an SMT-like architecture, similar to CUDA, to handle irregular parallel tasks.

points.h: Chips and models should be co-defined by the same company
points.body: Xiaomi partnered with MEMO to compress INT4 weights to 5 bits using a 5-value quantization method, with almost no accuracy loss, reducing memory bandwidth and capacity needs by 30%. The 3-billion-parameter MEMO model runs on the O3, with prefill performance up 40% and decode up 45%. This ability to co-define chips and models is the closed-loop advantage of vertical integration—no need to wait for others to define the model and then adapt a generic chip.

points.h: 3nm performance is eked out standard cell by standard cell
points.body: The O3 uses the more mature N3P process, delivering 5% higher performance at the same power and 5%-10% lower power at the same frequency. Xiaomi also made extensive process optimizations: self-developed standard cells increased from 480 in the O1 to over 2,400, covering various chip units; compressing the power supply buffer channel lets power and signals route from the middle of modules, boosting transistor density by 5%. The CPU changed from a 4-cluster to a 3-cluster 10-core all-big-core design, with single-core performance up 31% and multi-core up 60%, surpassing the A19 Pro.

points.h: Near-memory computing pushes phone memory bandwidth to 1.22TB/s
points.body: The Xuanjie O100 uses wafer-level 3D stacking: one compute wafer plus two memory wafers stacked vertically, interconnected via hybrid bonding, forming a near-memory computing architecture. It uses thousands of shorter, denser vertical connections to achieve high bandwidth with lower energy per bit shift—similar to HBM for phones. Data: 28,762 data connections, bandwidth 1.22TB/s, far exceeding the tens of bits of a traditional SoC-LPDDR connection. The compute layer has 14 independent cores, each paired with a RISC-V processor for control.

points.h: CXMT's value lies in co-definition, not speed grades
points.body: Xiaomi partners with CXMT to debut LPDDR6, reducing dependence on Samsung and SK Hynix. Even if CXMT offers the 10.667Gbps entry speed grade, Xiaomi can compensate for peak rate gaps with wider channels, larger SLC, and a custom memory controller. More importantly, the two companies co-validate and tune from the design stage, jointly defining a Chinese mobile memory subsystem solution. For CXMT, this proves its high-speed I/O and PHY capabilities, earning a seat at the next-generation mobile memory table.

points.h: Xiaomi is betting not on chips but on a time window
points.body: First, it bets on an on-device computing paradigm shift: AI's weight in SoCs is rising, phones become AI interaction gateways, and Xiaomi wants to stand in the definer's position. Second, it bets that vertical integration becomes a core competency for device companies—generic chips can't meet the fragmented needs of human, car, and home scenarios, so it must own its compute architecture. Third, it bets on an uncertain time window: trading resources for time, compressing the catch-up cycle, and preferring to bear engineering risk rather than wait for the window to close.

points.h: Xuanjie is closing faster, but still hasn't cleared any of three thresholds
points.body: Top-tier SoC companies need three capabilities: self-developed CPU/GPU microarchitecture, self-developed 5G baseband, and continuous multi-generation tape-outs with tens of millions of shipments. Xuanjie currently meets none, still clearly behind the first tier—it's just closing faster. What truly reshapes the industry isn't a single impressive chip, but a group of companies building sustained iteration capability. Xuanjie's greater significance is proving Xiaomi's chip efforts haven't stopped and that it's moving forward with Chinese chip industry partners.

terms.def: A cache shared by multiple compute units within a chip, like a shared water tank for a residential complex.
A wafer-level 3D stacking interconnect technology that uses direct copper-to-copper connections for high bandwidth and low power.
Placing memory and compute units close together to reduce data movement distance, improving bandwidth and energy efficiency.
A performance bottleneck where data movement capability limits performance, so adding more compute cores doesn't help.
A parallel processing architecture that can manage multiple task groups simultaneously to improve compute unit utilization.

quotes.text: To judge whether a company can really make chips, don't just stare at how many IP blocks it hand-crafts; you should look at how much system definition power it holds.
Xiaomi isn't slowly learning to make chips; it's trading resources for time, trying to build, within a limited time window, the full capability station that a mature chip company needs.
As long as data is stored reasonably and distributed efficiently, the entire chip can benefit.
Once it succeeds, you don't have to wait for someone else to define the model, then take a generic chip to adapt, and then figure out how to stuff it into a phone.
Better to bear more engineering and R&D uncertainty than to wait until the window truly closes and regret not having moved faster.
